cards.h: Eyes are tiny buckets of light
cards.b: Your pupil is about 7 mm wide. A big telescope mirror is metres wide. That collects millions of times more light, so you can see faint, distant objects and fine detail. The history of astronomy is a history of bigger, better light buckets and new colours of vision.

cards.h: The two jobs of a telescope
cards.b:
First, collecting power: how much light it gathers, proportional to the area of the main lens or mirror (so to diameter squared). Second, resolution: how fine a detail it can separate, which improves with larger diameter and shorter wavelength.

Magnification is the least important feature; without light and resolution it only blows up a blur.

Refractors use lenses. Hans Lippershey patented one in 1608; Galileo built his in 1609. Large lenses sag and give coloured fringes, so the biggest refractor ever is only 1 metre.

Reflectors use mirrors. Newton built one in 1668. Mirrors can be supported from behind and made huge. Every major modern telescope is a reflector.

Karl Jansky detected radio waves from the Milky Way in 1932, birthing radio astronomy. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes each show a different universe: cold gas, dust-hidden stars, million-degree gas.

Earth's air blocks most of these bands, so many telescopes must fly in space.

Air blurs stars (twinkling). Fixes: build on high dry mountains (Mauna Kea, the Chilean Atacama, Hanle in Ladakh), use adaptive optics (a deformable mirror that cancels turbulence hundreds of times a second), or go to space. The Hubble Space Telescope (1990, 2.4 m mirror) gave razor-sharp images above the air.

The James Webb Space Telescope launched 25 December 2021. It has a 6.5 m mirror of 18 gold-coated beryllium segments and sees infrared, which passes through dust and reveals very distant, redshifted galaxies. It sits near the Sun-Earth L2 point, 1.5 million km from Earth, behind a tennis-court-sized sunshield that keeps it near -233 C.

Next: the 39 m Extremely Large Telescope in Chile and the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope.

Link radio dishes across continents and they act like one giant telescope with the resolution of the whole span. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, linking telescopes around Earth, imaged the shadow of a black hole in galaxy M87. Telescopes now work as a network.

• 'The best telescope magnifies most.' Aperture decides.
  • 'Space telescopes are close to the stars.' They are still essentially at Earth's distance; they just avoid the air.
  • 'JWST replaced Hubble.' They complement: different wavelengths.

cards.h: From Kodaikanal to GMRT and Hanle
cards.b: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) near Pune has 30 dishes of 45 m each, built under Govind Swarup and opened in the 1990s: one of the world's most sensitive at low radio frequencies. The 2 m Himalayan Chandra Telescope at Hanle (4,500 m, Ladakh) sits in one of the world's driest, darkest sites. The 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope in Uttarakhand began working in 2016. ISRO's AstroSat (2015) was India's first dedicated astronomy satellite. LIGO-India was approved in 2023.

• Telescopes win on light-collecting area and resolution, not magnification.
  • Reflectors dominate; radio and space telescopes opened other wavelengths.
  • Adaptive optics and orbit beat the atmosphere.
  • JWST sees infrared from L2; networks of dishes can act as one giant telescope.

Think about it: (1) Why must infrared telescopes be kept very cold? (2) Why build GMRT in dozens of dishes instead of one huge one?
